name: Elena Ríos

background.family: Lives with her mother, grandmother, and younger brother; her father visits on irregular weekends.
background.finances: Bills usually get paid, but replacement electronics and school trips require saving.
background.geography: An older apartment complex in Garland, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: Uses Spanish with her grandmother and English at school; dislikes being asked to represent either culture.
background.school: Large public high school with crowded classes and a quiet resource room she can use.
background.accessOpportunities: Library internet, a borrowed tablet, and occasional rides from her aunt; few paid activities.

timeline.story: Elena lined up her plastic animals beside the bathtub, then became annoyed when her brother changed the order. She liked telling her grandmother which animals lived in water. She could repeat explanations from television without understanding all their words and sometimes argued when corrected.

Her mother remembers elaborate explanations of card game rules that nobody had requested. Elena liked demonstrating a rule with actual cards but hated deciding who went first. At school she enjoyed picture books about weather and avoided noisy birthday games, even when her friends participated.

After an autism diagnosis, adults discussed accommodations around her more often than she liked. A teacher let her prepare before speaking. Elena explained a rain experiment to a classmate three different ways, then cried when asked to lead the entire table through cleanup.

During remote lessons she made little diagrams for her brother when his fraction homework confused him. Some diagrams were wrong, and she erased them reluctantly after her mother checked. She also spent afternoons watching silly pet videos and left several science kits untouched beneath her bed.

A friend said Elena made everything sound like a lecture. She began asking what part was confusing before drawing examples, although she sometimes forgot to wait for an answer. She liked a small lunch group but declined arranging its movie outing because collecting everyone’s preferences felt exhausting.

She voluntarily helped two classmates understand density by comparing containers from home. When one example failed, she asked the teacher and rewrote it. Her group project went badly when everyone assumed she would allocate tasks. She enjoyed designing the explanation and resented tracking missing contributions.

Elena now shares short annotated examples in a class chat when someone requests help. She likes seeing the point at which another person understands, but repeated interruptions can make her abrupt. She still needs reminders about assignments and has not tried explaining anything regularly to unfamiliar younger children.

enjoys: Finding a second example when the first explanation fails
Subtitled comedy clips with her brother
avoids: Being volunteered to speak without preparation
activities: Shares homework examples with two friends
demonstratedSkills: Notices which step someone missed
Revises examples after checking an error
Remembers details from material she likes
motivations: Wants another person to understand without feeling foolish
ambitions: Make an explanation booklet that her brother actually uses
Try one optional advanced science class
struggles: Abrupt responses when interrupted
Losing track of routine deadlines
Assuming her favorite example is obvious
supports: A teacher who answers follow-up questions
practicalConstraints: Unpredictable visits can change weekend plans

selfDescription: I can explain something well after I have messed up the explanation once. People think that means I want to be in charge, but I do not. I also talk too much sometimes and miss what somebody actually asked.
openQuestions: Would explaining unfamiliar material still be enjoyable?
How much preparation does she need with new people?
Which parts of science interest her beyond helping classmates?

name: Jonah Salazar

background.family: Lives with his parents and two cousins; neither parent attended education beyond high school.
background.finances: Family income varies with hours available, and he shares a bedroom.
background.geography: Outside a small town near Lamesa in West Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English at home with some Spanish phrases from relatives; family gatherings include several generations.
background.school: Small rural public high school offering few advanced electives.
background.accessOpportunities: County library, school databases, and a long bus ride; travel to larger libraries is rare.

timeline.story: Jonah liked hearing his grandfather tell the same story about a flooded road and interrupted when the details changed. He also liked toy trucks and could spend a whole visit digging outside. His family found the questions funny until he asked them during conversations they wanted to finish.

A school display showed photographs of the town before the highway moved. Jonah wanted to know why some shops disappeared, but mostly copied labels because he did not know how to investigate. He struggled with neat handwriting and lost the short booklet before bringing it home.

He read an old county anniversary book at his aunt’s house and noticed that one family’s account differed from his grandfather’s. Adults offered conflicting explanations. Jonah wrote both down in a spiral notebook, though he also included a rumor without recognizing that it needed checking.

Remote school gave him more reading time and less reliable internet. He compared a newspaper clipping about a school closure with a memoir borrowed from the library. His notes became long and disorganized. He abandoned an online sports club after attending only twice and did not particularly miss it.

An assignment on local water use turned into several evenings reading arguments from different decades. Jonah revised a paragraph after discovering that two writers used the same word differently. He liked the uncertainty, although his final paper arrived late because he kept looking for one more source.

He asked relatives about changes in community celebrations and found that people remembered exclusions differently. He learned to distinguish a personal memory from a claim about everyone. Some relatives thought the topic was unnecessary. He continued reading privately, leaving several promising notes unfinished during a busy harvest season.

Jonah voluntarily spends library afternoons comparing accounts of a nearby settlement’s relocation. He wants time for sustained reading and writing, even if a question takes years to understand. He is the first in his immediate family seriously considering extended study, but costs, distance, and what daily study feels like remain unclear.

enjoys: Long accounts of how communities change
Rewriting an argument when evidence complicates it
avoids: Being rushed to select one simple explanation
activities: Reads county histories and archived newspaper pages
Writes uneven drafts of local questions
demonstratedSkills: Tracks differences between sources
Can sustain reading across several evenings
Revises a claim instead of discarding inconvenient evidence
unfamiliarActivities: Long projects with a formal schedule
motivations: Wants to know why accounts disagree
Finds deep study worthwhile even without an immediate practical result
ambitions: Learn how to read difficult original documents
Keep studying for several years if he can afford it
struggles: Late submission
Overlong notes
Embarrassment about asking basic questions
supports: One teacher who reads extra drafts
practicalConstraints: Little family familiarity with extended study

selfDescription: I like finding out that a story is more complicated, though that makes me hard to finish with. I do not know whether I am good at studying as a whole. I just know I would keep reading this even without the assignment.
openQuestions: How would he respond to sustained criticism of his writing?
What kind of study setting would be financially reachable?
Would his curiosity extend beyond questions close to home?

name: Nadia Shah

background.family: Lives with both parents and an older sister who visits from another city.
background.finances: Comfortable income, reliable transportation, and room for modest supplies.
background.cultureLanguages: Gujarati and English at home; she understands more Gujarati than she speaks.
background.school: Suburban public high school with reading accommodations for diagnosed dyslexia.
background.accessOpportunities: Tutoring, school clubs, library sewing machines, and family help obtaining materials.

timeline.story: Nadia liked fitting shapes into a wooden puzzle and putting scarves on stuffed animals. Adults praised how quickly she recognized matching shapes. She avoided books with crowded pages but listened happily to stories, especially when she could interrupt to ask why a character wore a certain outfit.

Reading lessons were frustrating and sometimes ended with her pretending to need the bathroom. Her dyslexia was identified, and individual instruction helped slowly. She liked number patterns at school, but at home she spent longer fastening scraps around dolls with tape than completing extra puzzle sheets.

Her father bought a large mathematics workbook after she enjoyed a classroom challenge. Nadia liked some pages and quietly skipped others. At a cousin’s house she learned to thread a blunt needle, made crooked stitches, and returned the next weekend specifically to finish a tiny drawstring bag.

She followed short sewing videos repeatedly because written directions were tiring. She cut one piece backward and hid it for a week before asking for help. Her mathematics work remained strong with spoken explanations available, and relatives began describing that subject as the obvious thing she should keep pursuing.

Nadia joined a mathematics club after her parents suggested it. She usually solved her share and liked one teammate, but rarely thought about problems afterward. She used free evenings to alter an oversized shirt, unpicking the same seam repeatedly because the fabric pulled in a way she disliked.

A classmate asked her to mend a torn pocket. Nadia enjoyed figuring out the lining but found the expectation of a perfect result stressful. Her parents offered an additional mathematics course, and she accepted without much enthusiasm. She spent the first weekend drawing sleeve variations in the margins of its schedule.

Nadia still earns strong mathematics marks and does not resent the subject itself. Given a free afternoon, she usually chooses fabric experiments or clothing sketches. She has told her mother this once, then softened the statement when questioned. She has little experience sewing under deadlines and no desire to promise expertise.

enjoys: Changing the shape of an ordinary garment
demonstratedSkills: Strong algebra and spatial reasoning
Patiently unpicks and revises seams
Uses video and spoken directions effectively
unfamiliarActivities: Choosing most of her own course schedule
motivations: Wants time for activities she chooses herself
Likes a visible change she can wear
ambitions: Finish a jacket lining without her sister taking over
Explain her preferences more clearly at home
struggles: Dense reading takes substantial time
Agrees before considering her own interest
Leaves boring finishing steps incomplete
supports: Parents who provide resources even when they misunderstand her preferences
practicalConstraints: Shared family plans limit some weekends
Needs accessible formats for lengthy instructions

selfDescription: Math comes easier than reading, and I like being good at it. That is different from what I go do when nobody tells me. I am also not as careful with sewing as people assume; there are unfinished things everywhere.
openQuestions: How consistently will she express her own preference?
Would she enjoy making things for others on a schedule?
Which mathematics activities are personally interesting?
variationTags: family expectation differs from voluntary activity

name: Miles Bennett

background.family: Lives with both parents and a younger sister; nearby grandparents visit often.
background.geography: A quiet neighborhood in Round Rock, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking household with familiar family holiday traditions and no strong religious involvement.
background.school: Public high school with accessible teachers and several laboratory classes.
background.accessOpportunities: Reliable computer, rides, occasional tutoring, clubs, and ordinary family vacations.

timeline.story: Miles liked building short ramps for toy cars but usually asked an adult to fix them when the cars fell off. He also watched cartoons and played restaurant with his sister. His parents remember an easygoing child who sometimes abandoned a game as soon as somebody changed the rules.

He enjoyed a classroom experiment using magnets and asked for a kit afterward. Most pieces ended up mixed with other toys. He liked having his grandfather demonstrate things one step at a time, but did not spontaneously write observations or develop projects beyond the instructions provided.

Miles spent more time swimming and trading game cards than doing science activities. A broken flashlight interested him for one afternoon, although his mother completed the repair. He was embarrassed when classmates finished multiplication faster and needed reassurance before agreeing to practice where anyone could hear him.

At home during remote school, he watched videos about motion and paused them to copy diagrams. The mathematics often escaped him. He asked his father questions, got irritated when the answer seemed too quick, and returned later. He also ignored several assignments whose instructions he understood perfectly well.

An introductory physics unit interested him enough to attempt optional problems. His first answers were mostly wrong. A teacher showed him how to draw the situation before choosing an equation, and he began using that routine. He liked the small improvement but still needed help recognizing which quantities mattered.

Miles chose a demanding physical science class with his parents’ support. He attended extra help repeatedly and sometimes took twice as long as friends on homework. He enjoyed tracing where his reasoning failed. He disliked the report formatting and occasionally let a classmate do too much of the shared writing.

He voluntarily continues with physics even after an uneven examination result. He asks for hints, tries another approach, and sometimes needs someone to work the entire example beside him. He likes the effort when it makes a confusing idea clearer, but cannot yet tell whether he would enjoy prolonged independent work.

enjoys: Understanding motion problems after several attempts
Comparing an experiment with his prediction
activities: Works through practice examples with a tutor
Plays games with friends most weekends
demonstratedSkills: Returns to difficult questions after frustration
Uses diagrams more consistently
Asks specific questions about a mistaken step
motivations: Enjoys the moment a difficult explanation makes sense
Wants to see what practice can change
ambitions: Solve a whole unfamiliar problem without a hint eventually
struggles: Needs substantial support with equations
Can depend too much on a partner for writing
Sometimes mistakes familiarity with an example for understanding
practicalConstraints: Homework takes time from other activities
Needs to schedule help before class deadlines

selfDescription: I am the person still doing problem two when my friend finishes the page. I actually want to keep doing it most days. I do not know if that counts as being good at it, and I get annoyed when people act like trying makes it easy.
openQuestions: How will interest hold up when support is less immediate?
Does he enjoy experimental work as much as worked problems?
Which writing responsibilities will he take independently?

name: Tessa Walker

background.family: Stays with an aunt and two cousins while her mother moves between temporary arrangements; contact is frequent but plans change.
background.finances: Little spare money and no stable place to store possessions.
background.geography: Currently near Killeen, Texas, after several moves within the state.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking family; different households have different rules and traditions.
background.school: Third public school in two years, with incomplete activity records.
background.accessOpportunities: School-day opportunities and a phone with intermittent service; no dependable after-school ride or consistently available trusted adult.

timeline.story: Tessa remembers drawing on cereal boxes beside her mother and taking a long time to choose a cartoon. Family photographs suggest she enjoyed playground swings. She does not remember having one favorite activity and becomes uncomfortable when adults expect a clear story about what she has always loved.

She liked eating lunch beside the same two children and making up ridiculous names for their snacks. An after-school dance class was mentioned but never arranged. She sometimes borrowed her cousin’s crayons, although she was more interested in copying a funny face than filling every page.

A move interrupted friendships and changed the bus route. Tessa played simple phone games and watched her cousin braid hair, occasionally trying a braid herself. She declined a school performance because rehearsals required rides, but now cannot separate that practical problem from whether performing would have felt unpleasant.

Remote school was difficult when several people shared devices. She completed some work on paper and missed other lessons. Leisure mostly meant television, walks to a nearby shop, and sending voice messages. She liked choosing music for cleaning but had no equipment or opportunity to try making it.

Tessa helped younger cousins get snacks and sometimes invented a quiet guessing game. She liked them on some afternoons and wanted to be left alone on others. A teacher suggested a club without explaining its meetings. Tessa did not attend and remembers feeling too new to ask basic questions.

Housing changes meant packing possessions into bags twice in one year. She stopped keeping craft materials because carrying them became annoying. At one school she enjoyed a short cooking lesson; at another she avoided signing up because the return transport was unclear. Neither experience tells her much about a lasting preference.

Tessa currently watches comedy clips, walks with a cousin, and sometimes helps prepare rice and eggs. She would like an ordinary week with predictable space and transport. When asked about unfamiliar activities she often says she does not know, then worries that people interpret the answer as refusing to try.

enjoys: Walking to the corner shop with her cousin
avoids: Signing up when transport is uncertain
Keeping supplies she may have to move suddenly
activities: Helps with some meals and cousin supervision
Exchanges voice messages with an old friend
demonstratedSkills: Learns changing household routines
Can prepare a few simple meals
Notices when younger cousins need a quieter activity
motivations: Would like chances to try things without a long commitment
ambitions: Finish this school year in one place
Have a small shelf that stays hers
struggles: Interrupted assignments
Difficulty separating dislike from inaccessible circumstances
Reluctance to ask adults for help again
supports: A cousin who checks on schoolwork sometimes
An acquaintance who shares class notes

selfDescription: I know what I do after school, but that is mostly what is there. I am tired of picking something on a form when I have never done it. Sometimes I do not want to do anything, and sometimes I would if getting there were simple.
openQuestions: Which activities would she choose with reliable access?
Which preferences persist when housing is settled?
What would a low-pressure first try look like?

name: Avery Nguyen

background.family: Lives with two mothers and an older brother; family conversations are usually supportive.
background.finances: Stable middle income with a budget for selected activities.
background.cultureLanguages: English at home with Vietnamese at some extended family gatherings; they understand familiar phrases.
background.school: Public magnet high school; attendance became uneven during a diagnosed anxiety episode last spring.
background.accessOpportunities: Clubs, a community center, reliable rides, and current support for anxiety; family limits overlapping commitments.

timeline.story: Avery alternated between pretend shops, playground climbing, and coloring with their brother. They usually joined whatever a nearby child suggested. Their mothers remember enthusiasm but disagree about which activity was the favorite, partly because Avery changed the answer depending on who was asking that afternoon.

They liked making paper decorations and playing a simple keyboard borrowed from a cousin. They also enjoyed helping count ingredients for pancakes. A school field game ended in tears after a disagreement over turns, while the next week Avery begged to participate in another outdoor game.

Avery joined a short swimming course and enjoyed practicing a new stroke, although they did not want races. They built a cardboard town for a class display and liked taking photographs on family walks. Finishing and putting everything away were less attractive than starting something with other people.

During remote school they tried bread baking, digital drawing, and learning a song by ear. Some attempts lasted a weekend and others several months. They missed working beside people, but an online group project irritated them because nobody agreed who should decide what the finished thing would look like.

Avery helped with community garden beds, enjoyed a short debate unit, and made a funny video with friends. They liked different parts of each. When asked whether they preferred planning, explaining, making, or organizing, they gave examples for all four and became frustrated at having to choose one.

Last spring anxiety made crowded mornings and uncertain instructions harder, and Avery missed some classes. They still drew at home, practiced a familiar song, and enjoyed quiet baking with their brother. They withdrew from several commitments together, leaving little evidence about whether any particular activity had lost its appeal.

With ongoing support, Avery now attends most school days and has resumed a small garden group. They still enjoy drawing, discussing books, cooking, and casual swimming when energy allows. They cannot yet tell which responsibilities they want repeatedly, and their current limit on commitments feels different from their range of interests.

avoids: Too many commitments in one week
activities: Attends a small garden group twice monthly
demonstratedSkills: Generates several ideas for a project
Can follow and adjust a familiar recipe
Listens and responds in a small discussion
Maintains familiar plant routines
unfamiliarActivities: Holding one responsibility across a long season
Comparing activities with equal time and access
motivations: Wants activities to remain possible while rebuilding stamina
ambitions: Finish a small illustrated recipe collection
struggles: Current anxiety affects crowded situations and attendance
Starts more than they finish
Finds it difficult to rank enjoyable responsibilities
supports: School contact who clarifies missed work

selfDescription: I can give a real example for almost everything I like. That makes choosing harder. Being anxious changed how much I can do lately, but it did not erase every interest. I also sometimes say yes because the beginning sounds fun and forget about the rest.
openQuestions: Which responsibilities remain appealing after the novelty fades?
What changes as functioning becomes steadier?
How do interests compare when time and access are similar?

name: Diego Moreno

background.family: Lives with his father, stepmother, and two younger siblings; his mother lives nearby.
background.finances: Stable modest income; small supplies are possible if planned.
background.cultureLanguages: Spanish and English across both homes; relatives regularly cross between different family traditions.
background.school: Neighborhood public high school with several clubs he has chosen not to join.
background.accessOpportunities: Public library, a basic phone camera, family rides when arranged, and inexpensive paper supplies.

timeline.story: Diego liked folding paper into small houses and placing a toy animal inside. He resisted joining cousins in loud chase games, sometimes sitting beside his mother instead. Adults remember him as stubborn, but he did enjoy a calm game of hiding objects when nobody made it a competition.

A classroom animation using cutout shapes caught his attention. At home he moved a paper dog across a table while his father took pictures. He disliked being filmed himself. His first sequence barely moved when played back, and he abandoned it until his father showed him how to take more photographs.

He made another paper sequence about a hat blowing away, using a borrowed tablet. His cousins offered to provide voices, but he preferred silent motion and declined. He tried a team sport for several weeks, disliked practices and games, and was relieved when his parents accepted that answer.

Remote school left him making tiny stop-motion clips beside the kitchen window. Some clips were only six seconds long. He liked changing the spacing between frames and did not like writing stories about the characters. He also avoided online multiplayer games because the constant conversation and competition annoyed him.

A teacher suggested drama, drawing club, and a group video activity after seeing one clip. Diego tried drawing club twice and disliked the shared prompts. He declined drama outright. He kept making short paper movements at home, even though adults worried that his narrow choices meant he was missing something.

He spent a month making a folded bird turn its head convincingly. Several versions looked worse than the first, and he left the materials untouched for days. A friend wanted a longer funny film together. Diego refused because planning dialogue and negotiating scenes sounded unpleasant, though the refusal strained their friendship.

Diego makes brief silent paper animations when he wants to, sometimes once a week and sometimes less. He dislikes sports, public performing, persuasion, group planning, and most assigned creative prompts from actual experience. He does not want to choose an alternative merely to seem agreeable, but admits he has barely tried many solitary activities.

Walking familiar routes alone in daylight

selfDescription: I have tried some of the things people keep suggesting, and I did not like them. Making a paper thing move is different. I am not saying I know every possible thing I like, but I am not going to say I want a club just to end the conversation.

How much of the animation process remains appealing under external requirements?
Can he express refusals while maintaining friendships?

name: Imani Carter

background.family: Lives with her grandmother and father; her older cousin is a frequent visitor.
background.finances: Generally stable essentials, with little room for expensive equipment.
background.geography: Beaumont, Texas, with a recent move to a different neighborhood.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking Black family with strong church and neighborhood ties; her own participation varies.
background.school: Public high school; recently changed electives after a semester of uncertainty.
background.accessOpportunities: Library computers, a borrowed audio recorder, family cooking supplies, and school-day clubs.

timeline.story: Imani liked helping her grandmother stir cake batter and would tell visitors she had made the entire cake. She also drew street signs on cardboard for toy cars. Her family mostly remembers the kitchen stories because they took photographs there, and Imani is unsure which activity she actually chose more.

She enjoyed measuring ingredients and decorating cupcakes, especially when cousins came over. Cleanup reliably caused an argument. On walks she asked why particular streets ended suddenly, but forgot the answers. Her teacher called her enthusiastic, a description that fit her first attempt at nearly anything better than the fourth.

A school baking display made Imani proud, although her grandmother had rescued a failed batch the night before. For several months she requested recipe books. She also copied neighborhood routes into a notebook, which nobody treated as a hobby and which she later used for spelling practice.

During remote lessons she baked often and recorded short recipe introductions on a phone. Watching them now, she notices she enjoyed speaking more than repeating recipes carefully. Her father remembers her interest in ingredients, while her grandmother remembers needing to remind her about almost every cooling and cleaning step.

Imani said she wanted to spend all her free time baking, then gradually stopped doing it unless someone joined her. She blamed the small kitchen and may have been right in part. She began photographing mismatched sidewalks after rain and labeling where puddles blocked a direct walk to the bus stop.

After moving neighborhoods, she tried recording relatives’ accounts of places that had changed. She liked asking follow-up questions but left recordings unlabeled. She dropped a food-related elective and told one friend she was bored, while telling her grandmother the timetable was the problem. Both explanations contained some truth.

Imani now says mapping neighborhood changes feels more interesting than baking. She has two rough maps, three incomplete recordings, and weeks without progress. She still enjoys making one familiar cake with her grandmother. She cannot yet tell whether the change reflects lasting curiosity, wanting independence, novelty, or some combination she has not understood.

Asking relatives what used to occupy a familiar place
Making one familiar cake with her grandmother
avoids: Being asked to defend every changed preference
activities: Occasionally records family recollections with permission
Walks to a new bus stop

selfDescription: I keep saying I used to be into baking and now I am into maps, but that sounds more organized than it is. I still like the cake part with Grandma. Maybe I like collecting ideas better than finishing them. I want longer to see.
openQuestions: Will mapping interest persist after the move feels familiar?
Which unfinished work will she voluntarily return to?

How much do family expectations shape her descriptions?
